ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: a×d instead of a×b×d — must know serial mediation algebra
ground_truth.original_snippet: Here, the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying each stage in the serial mediation process (a × b × d).
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Here, the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying the first and last stages in the serial mediation process (a × d).
ground_truth.description: Changed serial mediation formula from a*b*d (three paths) to a*d (two paths) — skips middle mediator link; estimate is wrong for serial mediation

matched_finding.subcategory: Hypothesis 2 indirect effect does not match the reported component paths
matched_finding.description: Hypothesis 2 indirect effect does not match the reported component paths: The reported indirect effect should be the product of the two unstandardized paths named in the paragraph. The displayed coefficients give .26 × .37 = .0962, which rounds to .10 rather than .07. Ordinary rounding cannot explain the gap: using the possible unrounded values behind .26 and .37 still gives a product around .093 to .099. If the .07 estimate comes from standardized paths, a different model, or unreported unrounded coefficients, state that and report those inputs. Otherwise, revise the indirect-effect estimate and its SE/CI/p-value.
matched_finding.quote:
As predicted and in support of Hypothesis 1, experienced patient incivility was positively related to negative emotions toward patients ( $\mathrm{B}=.26, \mathrm{SE}=.06, \mathrm{p}<.001$ ).

Hypothesis 2 predicted that the positive relationship between experienced patient incivility and compassion fatigue was indirect through negative emotions towards patients. Hypothesis 1 established support for the first step (path a) in this relationship. In the second step (path d), Time 3 negative emotions toward patients were positively related to Time 4 compassion fatigue $(\mathrm{B}=.37, \mathrm{SE}=.04, \mathrm{p}<.001)$. We then used MPlus' model constraint feature to estimate the indirect path $a \times d$. In support of Hypothesis 2, the positive indirect relationship between experienced patient incivility and compassion fatigue through negative emotions was significant $(\mathrm{B}=.07, \mathrm{SE}=.03, \mathrm{p}<.05,95 \% \mathrm{Cl}[0.02,0.14])$.

matched_finding.subcategory: Missing autoregressive controls in intro claims
matched_finding.description: Missing autoregressive controls in intro claims: The longitudinal claims are stronger than the analytic model appears to support. The results regress later constructs on earlier predictors, but Table 2 does not appear to include autoregressive controls for prior levels of the outcome constructs, such as earlier negative emotions, compassion fatigue, or enacted incivility. Without those controls, the analyses establish temporally separated associations, but they do not cleanly test change in the mediators or outcome over time.
matched_finding.quote: Within this paper, we (a) examine how experiencing incivility from customers is related to future enacted incivility towards customers, (b) identify affective and exhaustion-related mechanisms that drive these experienced-enacted relationships over time, and (c) examine the exacerbating role of a customer-based contextual factor, patient acuity, on these relationships.

ground_truth.modified_snippet: The scale items consisted of four negative emotions: (a) frustration, (b) irritability, (c) anger, (d) resentment.
ground_truth.description: Replaced discrete emotions (aversion, disgust, fear — high-arousal with specific appraisals) with irritation states (frustration, resentment) — different action tendencies and theoretical implications for incivility mechanism

matched_finding.description: Participant-flow arithmetic in Methods: The participant-flow arithmetic in the Methods section does not reconcile. The T4 count is $n=450$ and the final sample is $N=372$, which equals 78 quality exclusions, but the text also reports 16 exclusions for missing time points; additionally, the enumerated data-quality failures sum to 57 (56 inconsistent demographics + 1 high missingness), not 78.
matched_finding.quote:
Data were collected at four time points across four consecutive weeks, with each survey administered one week apart
(i.e., interval contingent sampling). Participants received a \$5 gift card for each survey they completed (with a possible \$20 total earned). The sample size and retention rates between each measurement time point were as follows: $\mathrm{n}=468$ nurses responded at time 1; n = 458 responded at time 2 ( $98 \%$ retention rate between T1 and T2); n = 454 responded at time 3 ( $98 \%$ retention rate between T2 and T3); and $\mathrm{n}=450$ responded at time 4 ( $98 \%$ retention rate between T3 and T4). Due to budgetary constraints, participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys (i.e., a participant who did not complete T2 survey was not sent the link for the T3 or T4 surveys). Participants who responded only to the T1 survey reported similar demographic information compared to those who completed all four time periods and had scale values on the key study constructs within one standard deviation of the means for the final sample of respondents who completed all four time periods - this suggests that the participants who did not complete all time periods were likely not substantially different from those included in the final sample.

Only participants who completed all four surveys ( $\mathrm{n}=16$ people excluded due to missing time points) and whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks ( $\mathrm{n}=78$ people excluded for poor data quality) were included in the final sample. Responses were considered failed data quality checks if they had any of the following characteristics: (a) demographic information was not consistent across measurement periods ( $\mathrm{n}=56$ people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age); or (b) missing values exceeded $50 \%$ of the questions ( $\mathrm{n}=1$ ). This resulted in a final sample size of $\mathrm{N}=372$.

matched_finding.subcategory: Misattribution of inflated correlations to within-person design
matched_finding.description: Misattribution of inflated correlations to within-person design: The very high bivariate correlations among several core constructs appear to warrant more direct treatment as a possible discriminant-validity and multicollinearity concern, rather than being attributed mainly to a diary or within-person design artifact. For example, Table 1 appears to show a correlation of about $.94$ between T4 compassion fatigue and T4 enacted incivility; even with the reported CFA support, correlations of this magnitude could affect interpretation of the sequential mediation paths.
matched_finding.quote: Additionally, diary studies of this nature may produce inflated correlations between variables within and across points in time due to the within-focused nature of the design (Beal, 2015). We acknowledge this particular issue in this study as some of the bivariate relationships are higher than convention. Future researchers may address this particular issue by integrating a latent multilevel framework that reduces potential serial and inflation effects by employing a within design that centers variables on the individual mean (Beal, 2015; Gabriel et al., 2019).

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Creates internal contradiction detectable within the paper
ground_truth.original_snippet: the stressor-emotion model of counterproductive work behavior (Spector & Fox, 2005). This model considers how environmental stressors and an individual’s perception of them are related to negative emotions and, ultimately, counterproductive work behaviors (CWB), such as enacted incivility.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: social learning theory (Bandura, 1977). This model considers how individuals learn behaviors through observation and modeling of others’ actions and their consequences, ultimately shaping counterproductive work behaviors (CWB), such as enacted incivility.
ground_truth.description: Replaced stressor-emotion model (emotional mediators) with social learning theory (observational learning) — but paper's mediators are negative emotions and compassion fatigue, not modeling/imitation

matched_finding.subcategory: Theory framing is unclear in the introduction
matched_finding.description: Theory framing is unclear in the introduction: The theoretical framing is somewhat unstable here: after identifying the stressor-emotion model as the primary lens, the next section briefly says the paper uses social learning theory but then describes the stressor-emotion sequence of stressor appraisal, negative emotions, and enacted CWB. It is not fully clear whether social learning theory plays an independent explanatory role or whether the experienced-to-enacted pathway is grounded mainly in the stressor-emotion model.
matched_finding.quote: To fill this gap in the literature, we primarily draw from the stressor-emotion model of counterproductive work behavior (Spector \& Fox, 2005), to support our investigation concerning the effect over time of experiencing incivility on nurses. Several tenets of this model (e.g., negative emotions as process mechanisms for the relationship between environmental stressors and enacted incivility) provided groundwork for the processes within our hypothesized relationships.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Grand-mean centering removed — must know this affects moderated mediation interpretation
ground_truth.original_snippet: Predictors in the moderated mediation model were centered at their respective grand means.
ground_truth.description: Deleted grand-mean centering — affects interpretability of conditional effects, multicollinearity of interaction terms, and meaning of simple slopes in moderated mediation

matched_finding.subcategory: Simple slopes are described as outcome levels rather than conditional associations
matched_finding.description: Simple slopes are described as outcome levels rather than conditional associations: The simple slopes test whether the incivility–negative-emotion association changes across levels of perceived acuity. They do not, by themselves, show that high-acuity employees report higher negative emotions at a fixed incivility score. Rewrite the hypothesis-test sentence around the conditional association: the positive relationship between experienced incivility and negative emotions is stronger at higher perceived acuity.
matched_finding.quote: Hypothesis 3 also predicted that the conditional relationship would be such that employees reporting higher perceived patient acuity would also report higher negative emotions. Simple slope analysis estimates at low ( $\mathrm{B}=.13, \mathrm{SE}=.12, \mathrm{p}=.26,95 \% \mathrm{Cl}[-0.10,0.35]$ ), medium ( $\mathrm{B}=.22, \mathrm{SE}=.09, \mathrm{p}<.05,95 \% \mathrm{Cl}[0.04,0.40]$ ), and high ( $\mathrm{B}=.32, \mathrm{SE}=.08, \mathrm{p}<.001,95 \% \mathrm{CI}[0.17,0.46]$ ) levels of the moderator revealed support for Hypothesis 3 .
